meta.title: Building Golden Datasets
meta.thesis: Building Golden Datasets is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A support bot needs a trusted set of examples that catches policy and citation mistakes. By the end, they should be able to build or review golden dataset card with inputs, expected outputs, and rubrics, measure coverage of top user intents and edge cases, and catch the failure where the dataset mirrors yesterday's easy demos and misses current failures.

mentalMap.title: Building Golden Datasets: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Build golden datasets from real workflows, expected evidence, slices, and failure labels rather than generic examples.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: A golden dataset is a living release contract: it preserves the behaviors and failures the product must remember.

modules.title: Golden cases preserve product expectations
modules.sub: They turn “do not break this” into data.
objectives: Record expected behavior and failure label.

blocks.title: Goldens are not random examples

spans.text: Problem anchor: a lesson generator once produced valid JSON with thin content and fake citations. A golden case captures the request, expected grounding, richness rubric, and failure label so the bug cannot quietly return.
A useful case includes input, setup fixtures, expected behavior, source evidence, severity, owner, and update notes.
Every golden case should say what regression it catches.

blocks.analogy: A golden case is a smoke alarm installed where a previous fire happened.

spans.text: Input: “Build a beginner lesson on RAG faithfulness.” Expected: source-backed explanation, big worked example, citation support, and beginner-level language. Failure label: unsupported citation.
The case is high severity because fake grounding damages trust.

items.text: Capture production failure or representative job.
Record input, fixtures, expected behavior, and severity.

options.text: It is always randomly generated.
It protects a specific product expectation or known failure from regression.
It has no expected behavior.

modules.title: Metadata turns examples into slices
modules.sub: Pass rates need categories and severity.

blocks.title: Averages hide where the product broke

spans.text: A 90% pass rate can hide that every advanced safety lesson fails or every beginner code example is too abstract. Slice metadata turns aggregate results into actionable insight.
Useful fields include topic, learner level, risk tier, tool path, retrieval mode, language, expected source, severity, owner, and last-reviewed date.
If someone cares about a subgroup, tag it.

blocks.analogy: Metadata is the label that lets you sort the evidence cabinet.

cells.text: Source IDs or facts that must support output.
Who updates the case and why.
Teams lower thresholds instead of fixing data.

blocks.title: Slice value
blocks.prompt: Why tag cases by learner level or risk tier?

options.text: So the model sees private metadata by default.
So aggregate pass rates cannot hide failures in important subgroups.
So every case has the same expected answer.

modules.title: Pair deterministic checks with judges
modules.sub: Goldens often need exact and semantic scoring.

blocks.title: Do not ask a judge to count brackets

spans.text: Use deterministic checks for schema, required fields, citation count, forbidden tools, and exact labels. Use an LLM judge for semantic criteria such as pedagogical fit, answer completeness, or richness.
A judge without evidence may approve a plausible hallucination, so pass retrieved sources or reference facts when judging groundedness.
One judge should answer one narrow question.

blocks.analogy: Use a ruler for length and a reviewer for taste.

spans.text: The harness checks JSON schema deterministically, then uses a calibrated rubric judge for richness and learner fit, passing source notes as evidence.
Failures are bucketed separately: schema, citation support, thin example, level mismatch.

items.text: Add narrow judge rubrics for semantic requirements.
Sample judge decisions for human calibration.

blocks.title: Scorer choice
blocks.prompt: What should validate required JSON fields?

options.text: Only a broad “is this good?” judge.
A deterministic schema or field assertion.
A public benchmark score.

blocks.explanation: Use exact checks where exact checks apply.

modules.title: A runner makes the dataset operational
modules.sub: Cases need to run against the real or faithful app path.
modules.summary: A golden dataset becomes useful when rerunnable.
objectives: Run cases through a task function.

blocks.title: Rerunnable beats impressive

spans.text: A runner executes the app path, applies scorers, stores trace IDs, and reports by slice. Even a tiny runner should separate case metadata from output scores.
Use the full production path when possible. If the suite uses fixtures or mocks, label them and keep contract tests for real integrations.
The report should show which case failed, why, and who owns it.

blocks.analogy: A dataset without a runner is a recipe nobody cooks.

blocks.title: Tiny golden dataset slice report
blocks.code:
cases = [
    {"id": "rag_beginner", "slice": "beginner", "must": "worked example", "output": "has worked example"},
    {"id": "safety_adv", "slice": "advanced", "must": "approval gate", "output": "mentions sandbox only"},
]
report = {}
for c in cases:
    passed = c["must"] in c["output"]
    bucket = "pass" if passed else "fail"
    report.setdefault(c["slice"], {"pass": 0, "fail": 0})[bucket] += 1
    print(c["id"], bucket.upper())
print(report)
blocks.explanation: The runner reports both individual failures and slice totals.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict which case fails.
predictThenReveal.answer: safety_adv fails because the output does not include the required approval gate.

blocks.title: Runner output
blocks.prompt: What should a golden dataset runner report besides overall pass rate?

options.text: Only the prettiest generated answer.
Failures by slice, severity, scorer, and trace/case ID.
Only token count with no case IDs.

modules.title: Keep goldens alive without overfitting
modules.sub: Datasets rot when products and policies change.

blocks.title: A stale golden can be worse than no golden

spans.text: When source content changes, expected answers may become stale. Update the dataset with a dated rationale, not by quietly lowering thresholds.
When production incidents occur, add minimal cases that would have caught them. Avoid overfitting by holding out cases, sampling human review, and checking real user outcomes.
Every case needs an owner and a reason to exist.

blocks.analogy: A golden dataset is a garden, not a monument.

blocks.title: Verify a golden dataset before release

spans.text: Review the dataset as a product artifact.

items.text: Cases come from representative workflows, known failures, or named coverage gaps.
Each case has expected behavior, evidence, severity, owner, and slice metadata.
Scorers match requirements and semantic judges are calibrated.
Stale cases are updated with dated rationale.
Production incidents feed new minimal regression cases.

blocks.title: Dataset lifecycle
blocks.prompt: What should happen when a golden answer becomes stale because the product changed?

options.text: Delete the whole suite silently.
Update the case with a dated rationale and rerun baselines.
Lower the pass threshold without notes.

eval.label: Eval
eval.laymanDefinition: A repeatable test of model or system behavior against expected criteria.
eval.technicalNote: In these lessons, evals are release evidence: they combine cases, assertions, scores, and review rules.

trace.label: Trace
trace.laymanDefinition: A structured record of one run, including spans, inputs, outputs, metadata, and scores.
trace.technicalNote: Traces make failures diagnosable by showing which retrieval, model, tool, or scoring step produced the result.

dataset.label: Dataset
dataset.laymanDefinition: A curated set of examples used for evaluation, debugging, or regression checks.
dataset.technicalNote: A useful eval dataset stores inputs, expected behavior, metadata slices, and source or rubric references.

judge.label: LLM-as-judge
judge.laymanDefinition: An LLM used to grade or compare outputs with a rubric.
judge.technicalNote: LLM judges are semantic scorers, not final authority; their prompts, model, thresholds, and spot checks must be versioned.

regression.label: Regression
regression.laymanDefinition: A previously working behavior that breaks after a prompt, model, data, or code change.
regression.technicalNote: Regression testing protects known capabilities and safety boundaries while allowing harmless wording variation.

rubric.label: Rubric
rubric.laymanDefinition: A scoring guide that states what a good answer or run must demonstrate.
rubric.technicalNote: Rubrics make qualitative judgment reviewable by naming criteria, severity, examples, and thresholds.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: A golden case for a customer-support bot includes the input 'How do I reset my password?', the expected output, and a failure label of 'wrong_steps'. What is the PRIMARY purpose of that failure label?

options.text: To tell the runner which model version produced the output
To categorize what kind of problem occurred so failures can be grouped and acted on
To set the severity score for the slice automatically
To trigger a judge rubric instead of a deterministic check

questions.explanation: A failure label names the type of failure (e.g., 'wrong_steps'), which lets you group and triage failures systematically rather than reading every output by hand.

questions.prompt: Your golden dataset has a 'region' metadata field. After a run, the overall pass rate is 91 %, but the pass rate for region = 'APAC' is 61 %. What does this slice-level view let you do that the overall number hides?

options.text: Detect that a specific subgroup is underperforming so you can investigate or block the release for that slice
Automatically retrain the model on APAC examples
Replace deterministic checks with judge rubrics for APAC cases
Increase the severity score of all APAC cases to 'critical'

questions.explanation: Slice-level pass rates surface hidden regressions in subgroups; a healthy aggregate can mask a badly failing segment that would harm real users.

questions.prompt: You are checking whether a refund-policy response contains the exact phrase 'within 30 days'. Which approach is most appropriate for this check, and why?

options.text: A judge rubric, because exact phrasing requires nuanced semantic understanding
A deterministic check (e.g., substring match), because the criterion is precise and unambiguous
A human review queue, because no automated check can handle policy text
A semantic similarity score, because string matching is too brittle for production

questions.explanation: Deterministic checks are ideal when the pass/fail criterion is exact and objective — a substring match is fast, free, and perfectly reliable for a known required phrase.

questions.prompt: When the runner executes your golden dataset, it stores a trace ID alongside each result. In one or two sentences, explain what a trace ID is for and how it helps after a failure is detected.
questions.acceptableAnswer: A trace ID is a unique identifier linked to a specific run of a case that lets you look up the full execution log or trace for that case. When a failure is detected, you use the trace ID to retrieve the exact inputs, outputs, and intermediate steps that produced the failure, making debugging faster and more precise.
questions.explanation: Trace IDs connect a summary failure report back to the full execution record, so engineers can inspect exactly what happened instead of re-running the case blind.

questions.prompt: After a production incident, your team adds a new golden case that reproduces the bug. Six months later, the product behavior intentionally changes and that case now fails correctly. What should you do — and what should you NOT do?

options.text: Delete the case silently so the suite stays green; old incidents are no longer relevant
Update the expected output with a rationale note explaining why behavior changed; do not remove the case without documentation
Keep the case failing permanently as a reminder of the incident
Duplicate the case and tune the expected output until the overall pass rate exceeds 95 %

questions.explanation: Updating a stale case with a written rationale preserves institutional memory of the incident while keeping the suite accurate — silently deleting or ignoring it risks overfitting the suite to current behavior without understanding why it changed.
